articles.title: Belkin’s cheap wired earbuds give you ANC without battery anxieties
articles.summary: Belkin is launching four new affordable earbuds, including a wired option that provides active noise cancellation for USB-C devices.
articles.body: Belkin is launching four new affordable earbuds, including a wired option that provides active noise cancellation (ANC) for users who don’t want to worry about battery life. The SoundForm USB-C Wired Earbuds with ANC will be available sometime in October for $34.99, according to Belkin’s press release, and come in white or black. They feature a 4-foot-long cable with a built-in microphone and volume adjuster toggle, and carry an IPX5 rating — meaning the earbuds can survive being splashed with water. The cable is flat to help prevent tangles. They provide 12mm audio drivers and three equalizer presets to adjust the listening experience. Belkin’s wired SoundForm earbuds draw power for the ANC feature from whatever device it’s connected to. [Image: The flat cable design should help to prevent it from getting tangled in your pocket. The rest of Belkin’s new earphone products are wireless and will all be available for $34.99 “beginning September 2025,” according to Belkin. The SoundForm Rhythm ANC includes 10mm drivers and two microphones per earbud, Bluetooth 5.3 support, an IPX5 rating for splash resistance, and three listening modes: ANC, Hear-Thru, and Standard. The earbuds last up to eight hours per charge, with up to 20 additional hours of playtime provided by the included charging case. [Image: [Image: [Image: The SoundForm ActiveFit feature silicone ear hooks to keep them in place during physical activity, as well as a water and dust-resistant IP54 rating. You don’t get any ANC features, but they do include Standard and Hear-Thru listening modes for training in both indoor and outdoor environments. The ActiveFit batteries provide up to nine hours of playback, with up to 27 additional hours provided by the case. The SoundForm Anywhere is the most compact of Belkin’s new earbud launches, featuring multipoint connectivity for pairing with two devices and up to 26 hours of total battery life — six provided on a single charge, and 20 from the charging case.

articles.title: Boston Dynamics’ Tesla Bot rival Atlas will start building Hyundai cars in 2028
articles.summary: Hyundai unveiled the latest version of Boston Dynamics’ Atlas robot with increased degrees of freedom. The new robot will go to work at Hyundai’s factories starting in 2028.
articles.body: Boston Dynamics unveiled the latest version of its humanoid Atlas robot Monday at CES in Las Vegas. The robot, with a glowing circle for a face, a fully electric, battery-powered body, and joints that can rotate 360 degrees, is so advanced that it will soon be working alongside human factory workers for parent company Hyundai, the companies claimed. Hyundai said it plans on mass-producing Atlas as “production-ready humanoid robots” that will be put to work at the automaker’s car plants, starting with the Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant in Savannah, Georgia. The company estimates it will produce 30,000 robots annually starting in 2028. The company also plans on putting the first Atlas robots to work that year “on processes with proven safety and quality benefits, such as parts sequencing.” By 2030, Hyundai says that Atlas will level up to tasks involving “repetitive motions, heavy loads, and other complex operations.” The automaker envisions a “harmonious collaboration between humans and robots,” despite widespread fears about job losses as a result of increased automation. [Media: Hyundai kicked off its keynote with a K-pop dance number featuring its Spot robots (which lasted about as long as one of the robots took to open a door afterward). The star of the show was a remotely-piloted Atlas prototype making its public debut. A future production model that will actually be rolling out to Hyundai and other customers was also shown off, albeit static and non-working. The polished product version of Atlas will be water resistant and capable of withstanding temperatures down to -4 degrees and up to 104 degrees Fahrenheit. It also features tactile sensing in its hands and will swap out its own batteries when they start running low. It had less exposed wiring than the prototype and baby blue panels covering some parts of its body. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Boston Dynamics started as a spin-off from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 1992. The company used funding from DARPA to create robots like BigDog, but is best known for the viral fame its robots have found online. Its two main stars have been Atlas, a humanoid bipedal robot that can run and do backflips, and Spot, a smaller quadrupedal “dog” that’s been tested in a variety of scenarios, from sheep herding to assisting health care workers during the pandemic. The company started selling Spot in June 2020 for $74,500, targeting businesses looking for an automated way to patrol and inspect warehouses. Despite the viral fame, Boston Dynamics has consistently lost millions of dollars annually for a number of years. Hyundai acquired Boston Dynamics in 2021 in a deal that valued the company at $1.1 billion. The automaker has long predicted that robots will become an increasingly noticeable presence at its factories over time. And with today’s demonstration, Hyundai is hoping to prove that its robot is more advanced and more capable of performing physical tasks than rivals like Tesla’s Optimus robot. Tesla has ridden a wave of AI hype in recent years to a market capitalization of over $1 trillion, over 15 times Hyundai’s value, despite selling vastly fewer cars. The shift for Atlas from research platform to commercial robot is certainly a significant milestone for Boston Dynamics and its parent company. It’s also likely to be an extremely costly endeavor for Hyundai to put Atlas into volume production. The companies haven’t said how much Atlas costs to manufacture, but Boston Dynamics does sell its Spot robots for around $75,000 a unit. Atlas is estimated to be hundreds of thousands of dollars more expensive. Hyundai claims its supply chain, access to advanced manufacturing facilities, and previous work on AI-based software and software-defined vehicles give it a unique advantage that will enable it to scale up its robot production while also keeping costs low. [Image: [Image: Those costs are likely to rise as Atlas becomes more dextrous and autonomous. Hyundai said that the latest, all-electric version of the robot has 56 degrees of freedom (DoF), up from the 50 DoF that was reported in April 2025. The robot has fully rotational joints and “human-scale hands with tactile sensing” and is engineered to handle tasks autonomously. It can be taught “most tasks” in a day, can replace its own batteries automatically for all-day continuous use, and can lift up to 110 pounds (50kg). It’s also water resistant and can operate in temperatures as low as -4 and as high as 104 degrees Fahrenheit (20 to 40 degrees Celsius). For years, Boston Dynamics has impressed with demonstrations of its dexterous biped bots performing cartwheels, breakdances, and barrel rolls. Still, the news that Hyundai is on the cusp of putting Atlas to work at its factories may change the public’s perception of the seemingly friendly robot, especially if it emerges as a potential Terminator of jobs. Amazon, for example, is hoping its robots can replace more than 600,000 jobs in the US by 2033, according to recently leaked strategy documents. Hyundai has said that by 2028, its $21 billion investment in the US will create 14,000 jobs directly, and more than 100,000 if indirect jobs are included. Hyundai is also announcing a partnership with Google’s DeepMind AI research lab to combine Boston Dynamics’ robotic expertise with Google’s AI foundation models. The automaker is also sourcing AI chips and software from Nvidia. Of course, shifting from impressive demos to a working product that can justify its enormous costs will be an equally enormous challenge for Hyundai and Boston Dynamics. There is a lot of hype around humanoid robots, and not a lot of evidence that they’re worth the complexity and effort to build them — yet. With additional reporting by Stevie Bonifield

articles.title: Why Waymo is having a hard time stopping for school buses
articles.summary: ﻿By trying to drive more assertively, Waymo appears to be adopting some dangerous human habits.
articles.body: For years, Alphabet-owned Waymo has tried to set itself apart from other self-driving startups by emphasizing a culture of caution and safety. Now, just ahead of major planned rollouts across the country, it is facing a recurring failure in one of the most sensitive places imaginable: school zones. In December, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened an investigation into Waymo after Austin’s largest school district reported at least 19 incidents where the company’s robotaxis failed to fully stop for school buses during loading and unloading — an illegal violation in all 50 states. Waymo quickly responded by issuing a voluntary software recall and rolling out updates intended to fix the problem. But the patch didn’t work. Since the update, Austin Independent School District (ISD) says at least four additional violations have occurred, including one as recently as January 19th, when a Waymo vehicle was filmed breezing through the opposite lane of traffic as children waited to cross the street and board a bus with its stop arm extended. In total, at least 24 safety violations involving Waymo vehicles and school buses have been reported in Austin since the start of the 2025 school year. [Media: Waymo has defended itself, in part, by noting that none of the Austin school bus incidents resulted in a collision or injury. But that’s no longer strictly the case nationwide. Last week, Waymo published a blog post acknowledging that one of its vehicles struck a child outside a Santa Monica elementary school on January 23rd. Although the school district told The Washington Post that the child sustained only minor injuries, the outcome could have been far worse: Waymo says the vehicle slowed from 17 mph to 6 mph in the instant before impact. Experts specializing in autonomous vehicle safety and pedestrian interaction told The Verge that these incidents were concerning, particularly given the company’s stated goal of making its vehicles drive more “confidently assertive.” In an effort to shed the stereotype of driving like a cautious grandparent, the vehicles have been spotted playing looser with traffic rules. But making robotaxis seem more humanlike also risks having them inadvertently inherit some of our more dangerous driving habits. [Media: “These technologies are still being developed and tested in a real world environment because there’s a lot of things that happen in the real world that’s hard for companies and engineers to anticipate,” Cornell Tech professor and expert in human-robot interaction Wendy Ju tells The Verge. “Unless you have some understanding of all the things that might happen, it’s hard to know what to design around.” Waymo did not respond to repeated requests for comment. On Wednesday, Waymo’s chief safety officer Mauricio Peña responded to safety concerns raised during a Senate hearing. He said Waymo is evaluating each of the school bus incidents and is developing fixes, some of which have already been incorporated into its software. Peña also said they are working with Austin ISD to “collect data on different lighting patterns and different conditions.” Waymo notably didn’t commit to stop operating around school buses while that data collection and testing occurs. School bus stops put autonomous vehicle ‘logic’ to the test Navigating around school buses is one of the more dangerous aspects of driving, for both humans and robots alike. NHTSA attributed 61 fatalities to vehicles illegally passing school buses between 2000 and 2023, almost half of whom were pedestrians under the age of 18. That danger has less to do with the bus drivers themselves, who are typically licensed and careful, and more to do with the chaotic, improvisational nature of the situation. Buses are often double-packed, and kids, being kids, might not wait to cross the street when they are supposed to. “Waymos are having an issue because every driver has issues around school buses,” Ju said. As a result, drivers navigating around buses need to rely on experience and intuition in addition to following the firm set of rules they learned in driver’s ed. That kind of common-sense logic, which comes naturally to skilled human drivers, Ju says, is particularly challenging for self-driving cars. “There’s all these moments in time where you actually have to make a judgment call between different things that you’re supposed to do,” Ju said. Waymo running a ‘public beta test’ with pedestrians? On a technical level, there may be more at play. According to George Mason University professor and director of the Mason Autonomy and Robotics Center Missy Cummings, the apparent spike in robotaxi safety issues involving school buses may be linked to what she describes as Waymo’s increasing shift away from traditional, modular machine-learning toward a greater emphasis on end-to-end learning, a technology she calls “faddish” and “still nascent.” Waymo, publicly, says it uses a mixture of the two, but some speculate that that balance is shifting. Earlier autonomous-vehicle systems relied on more conservative, layered architectures, with separate modules responsible for detecting objects, classifying them, and applying explicit safety rules governing how a vehicle should respond. End-to-end learning, by contrast, collapses much of that process into a single model that takes in all of the information gathered by a car’s sensors at once and produces driving decisions probabilistically, based on patterns learned from large swaths of human driving behavior. The result is something that can seem more “natural” and humanlike, though Cummings argues it can also introduce additional risk, especially in high-stakes scenarios like school bus stops. The safety incidents demonstrate “all the hallmarks of problems when you change architecture,” Cummings said. “I suspect many [robotaxi companies] are doing it.” Schools asked Waymo to pause Regardless of what is causing the mistakes, Austin ISD has made its position clear. Officials reportedly asked Waymo to cease robotaxi operations around schools during loading and unloading hours until the issue is resolved. But Waymo refused and has continued operating, a decision experts say seems both shortsighted and at odds with the company’s public image of promoting safety and caution. “I think it’s concerning that Waymo wouldn’t agree to that,” Cummings said. “You’re only talking about truly an hour and a half, 45 minutes in the morning and 45 minutes in the afternoon, so it’s not a heavy lift to not do that.” Philip Koopman, a Carnegie Mellon Professor and AV safety expert, echoed that sentiment in a recent edition of his Substack newsletter Autonomous System Safety. “Waymo is making an explicit choice to gamble with children’s lives,” Koopman writes. “They say they like the odds, but it is not their gamble to make.” And while the vast majority of issues involving school buses occur in Austin, that’s likely partly due to the city recently outfitting each of their stop arms with cameras. In other words, similar incidents could be happening elsewhere but are simply going unnoticed. Austin ISD did not respond to our requests for comment. (Axios reported that the problem is happening in Atlanta as well.) The school bus incidents, along with the striking of the child in California, have sparked three federal investigations in as many months. Though unlikely in Texas’ loose AV regulatory environment, incidents like these could put Waymo at risk of having its operating license revoked. Even now, as investigators reportedly head to Austin in person to probe the company, robotaxis continue to operate in the school zone. At the very least, that cavalier approach could make other municipalities think twice before welcoming the company’s cars to their streets. “Waymo brought this on themselves,” Cummings said. “If they had done the responsible thing and self elected to stay out of school zones until they fixed it, then they wouldn’t have this big [public] investigation because the big investigation is made public.”

articles.title: Kyunki Papa Kehte Hain actor Raj Anadkat: ‘Diwali teaches me to never lose hope, there is always light at the end of the tunnel’
articles.summary: Currently seen as Pawan Parik in Yash and Mamta Patnaik’s Kyunki Papa Kehte Hain, Raj Anankat speaks about his Diwali plans, balancing work and family and
articles.body: Currently seen as Pawan Parik in Yash and Mamta Patnaik’s Kyunki Papa Kehte Hain, Raj Anankat speaks about his Diwali plans, balancing work and family and the importance of spreading happiness.Diwali is a festival of hope, positivity and fresh beginnings. For actor Raj Anadkat, the festival means a lot as it teaches him to remain positive and keep going irrespective of what life throws at him. The actor is currently seen playing the character of Pawan Parik in Kyunki Papa Kehte Hain. The actor has a rather busy festive season this year with the actor’s shooting commitments keeping him busy throughout the month.“Diwali teaches me a lot of things,” Raj says about what Diwali means to him. It reminds me to never give up. Never lose hope. No matter how dark it may get, there is always a light at the end of the tunnel. That is something I really believe in and I think it is a beautiful message the festival brings with it.”The actor was supposed to celebrate the festival with his family, but his professional commitments have caused a change in his schedule. “I’m playing the lead in my show so I’ll be shooting throughout the month,” he says honestly. I had arranged to do something with my family earlier but unfortunately had to cancel due to work commitments. But, I’m hoping I get some time with them to celebrate.”Though Raj has a busy schedule, he ensures that he maintains a balance between his professional and personal life. “I try to balance my work and personal life as well as I can. If I get off early I hurry home to spend time with my family or take them out to a nice dinner. We are also like a family on set so it’s just as fun to celebrate these moments together,” he adds.Diwali is always a bagful of memories for Raj but this year he is excited to celebrate with his Kyunki Papa Kehte Hain team. “Every Diwali is memorable in its own way but I have a feeling that this year is going to be extra fun with my Kyunki Papa Kehte Hain team,” he says.Sending out a heartfelt message to his fans this festive season, Raj concludes, “I just want everyone to remember to be kind, be a spark in someone’s life and support each other’s growth. Be happy with other people and see to it that you make other people happy with you. Sometimes the smallest gesture can light up one’s life. So just be happy, live and let live. Wishing you all a very, very happy Diwali!"Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: If Snap's Specs are still ridiculously expensive, they're also a lot more comfortable than they used to be | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Snap's Specs, which have been in development for many years now, are going to market this fall. Will they be a hit with users?
articles.body:
When I tried a prototype of Snap’s Specs at CES in Las Vegas earlier this year, the experience left something to be desired. The company’s AR glasses — which the company calls a “new kind of computer” — were heavy (they weighed around 8 ounces) and fit rather uncomfortably on my face. The device was also hot, and made my face feel tingly — a common side-effect of smart glasses where massive computing is happening under the hood.

Fast forward to late October, when I met back up with the Snap team at a Four Seasons in downtown San Francisco. By this time, the company had debuted Specs publicly during an event with CEO Evan Spiegel, and pre-orders of the company’s long-gestating headset were already underway.

What I can say is this: Specs has improved the form factor significantly since my first brush with the device. The glasses now weigh nearly half of what the previous version did, slimming down to 132 grams, or approximately 4.6 ounces. They were quite comfortable and, during the hour-ish that I demo-ed the device, it did not heat up like the previous version had.

Specs now comes in two sizes — 47mm and 52mm. The purpose here is purely to accommodate different head sizes, ensuring the glasses fit snugly on whoever’s face happens to be wearing them. They also now come equipped with spring hinges, which make the device more flexible and comfortable.

However, if the body of the device has improved greatly, its soul is still a work-in-progress. The glasses can be fun — but they also still seem to lack a dedicated purpose, and one struggles to imagine how, specifically, this expensive head gear ($2,200 a pop) would prove useful in a daily capacity. When I asked Snap staff what the device was really for — fun and games or productivity — the answer was vague. The device attempts to be a bunch of things at once and, in the process, ends up feeling a little rudderless.

I have racked my brain to come up with some daily use-cases for Specs. Some of the things I came up with were:

Watching TV or movies while you’re on a train or some other form of public transportation . There are places where you just have to hang out for awhile and, not infrequently, one way to pass the time is streaming. Specs provides a much more immersive form of mobile entertainment than simply watching a video on your cell phone. The device’s integrations with HBO Max and YouTube make it an appealing entertainment option for users who are in-transit.

Reading . Because of the immersive nature of Snap’s headset, I feel like they could be a good option for reading while traveling. When you’re reading with Specs, it feels like you’re locked into whatever text you happen to be looking at. It weirdly helped me focus. An integration for newspapers or Kindle could make the glasses a good way to read while you’re mobile (I’m envisioning the ideal setting being on a plane, train, or the back of a car).

Taking easily shareable weird videos . Like many of Meta’s smart glasses, Specs allows users to take photographs and videos, which is an odd but fun component of the user experience. The ability to generate GoPro-like videos and easily text them to your friends is something that I could see the casual user doing on a somewhat regular basis.

By contrast, here are some of the areas I’m still not totally sold on as Specs use-cases:

Specs as a daily workspace and productivity tool . Snap is selling Specs as a way to work. The company claims its headset can “transform almost any location into an immersive, flexible workspace.” However, I have a really hard time imagining Specs being something that the average worker is going to want to incorporate into their workflows. It’s less convenient to strap the glasses to your head than it is to simply sit at your computer typing. What can Specs provide that a cell phone and laptop can’t? The social stigma of wearing weird, large glasses and gesticulating to operate them would also seem to be a deterrent.

A widely used gaming device. Due to the prohibitive cost of the device (again, nearly $2200), I have a really hard time imagining that there is going to be a huge audience for Specs as a gaming device. Most Xboxes are under half the price of this device. Are the games on Specs fun? Sure, kind of. But are teenagers going to be clamoring for them come Christmas time? That I’m not so sure about.

Specs is impressive for how the Snap team has managed to integrate a variety of user experiences into one unified device. There are a lot of impressive achievements here — specifically the spatial synching tech that allows two users to see the same thing simultaneously — that, with some further development, could be deployed towards some really interesting use cases.

The bottom line is that Snap’s device can continue to grow and transform as the company iterates. It’s an interesting product that — like a lot of its peers — doesn’t necessarily seem to have a clear purpose but, in time, could become many things.

What the device currently offers, however, may not be compelling enough to encourage people to shell out the cash that Snap is asking for.

articles.title: Bigg Boss Malayalam 8: Mohanlal makes surprise entry into the house for Diwali celebrations; contestants receive special gifts
articles.summary: Diwali celebrations turned extra special for the contestants of Bigg Boss Malayalam Season 8 as host Mohanlal made a surprise entry into the house while
articles.body: Diwali celebrations turned extra special for the contestants of Bigg Boss Malayalam Season 8 as host Mohanlal made a surprise entry into the house while the episode was underway. The unexpected visit brought excitement and happiness to the housemates, who got an opportunity to celebrate the festival with their favourite host.The celebrations began with a special task announced for the 14 contestants. They were asked to split into two groups and prepare jalebis with the Malayalam phrase 'Ee Deepavali Adhi Manoharam' written on them. Mohanlal announced that the team that completed the task better would receive a special gift. While the contestants were busy preparing the festive sweets, an unexpected moment unfolded as Mohanlal entered the house through the storeroom.The housemates were visibly surprised and excited to see the actor. They welcomed him with Diwali greetings and exchanged festive wishes. Mohanlal then visited the kitchen area, where he checked out the jalebis prepared by both teams and even tasted them. Appreciating their efforts, he later decided to take a tour of the house. During his visit to the bedroom and other areas, Bigg Boss also welcomed Mohanlal back to the house and extended Diwali wishes to him.After visiting the different areas, Mohanlal joined the contestants in the living room and shared a few words of advice. He encouraged them to focus on their gameplay and discuss their strategies more openly. He also called Gautham Sasi over and asked him to sit beside him. The warm interaction, with Mohanlal holding Gautham's hand while speaking to him, turned into one of the sweetest moments of the celebrations.Mohanlal then asked Shijin to sit beside him and appreciated his successful execution of the Atom Bomb heist. He described it as a remarkable heist unlike anything previously witnessed in Bigg Boss Malayalam. Referring to Gautham and Shijin's involvement in the task, Mohanlal jokingly said that he was sitting between two thieves. Gautham had carried out the first theft, while Shijin had completed the second heist.Following the appreciation, Mohanlal announced that both teams had performed well in the jalebi task. He asked the contestants to collect their gifts from the storeroom. The housemates were pleasantly surprised to find framed family photographs inside the gift packages. As they opened their presents, each contestant excitedly shared pictures of their loved ones with Mohanlal.The celebrations continued in the activity area, where the contestants had arranged special performances for their host. Wikky Thug started the entertainment with a song from the film Urumi, with Vipin joining him to provide the musical accompaniment. Mohanlal appreciated their performance. Shijin and Mridhula followed with a dance performance, creating a festive atmosphere despite the controversies surrounding them. The host also appreciated their performance.Gautham Sasi was the next performer. Known for his stand-up comedy, he presented a special segment connecting different contestants with various kinds of crackers. His entertaining act added another cheerful moment to the Diwali celebrations, with Mohanlal appreciating his efforts.The celebrations reached another high point when Bigg Boss announced that it was time to burst crackers. The contestants joined Mohanlal with sparklers, making the festive occasion even more memorable.However, the celebrations eventually came to an end when Bigg Boss announced that it was time for Mohanlal to leave. His departure also coincided with Nowfina's farewell, making the occasion an emotional one for the housemates.While the Diwali celebrations brought a refreshing break from the usual tensions inside the house, the upcoming episodes are expected to shift the focus back to the competition. articles.title: Instagram’s AI age detection is expanding globally
articles.summary: Meta is globally expanding the age estimation technology it uses to find teenagers on Instagram who haven’t correctly disclosed their age.﻿
articles.body: Meta is globally expanding the age estimation technology it uses to find teenagers on Instagram who haven’t correctly disclosed their age. The rollout will automatically place “millions more teens on Instagram into Teen Account protections,” according to Meta’s announcement, after launching the AI-powered age assurance updates in the US, EU, and Brazil last year. The age detection tools proactively look for signals that likely determine whether Instagram users are under 18 years old, and automatically place users between 13 and 17 under more restrictive Teen Accounts, even if they signed up using a fake adult birthday. Teen Accounts are designed to provide a safer and more age-appropriate experience by being private by default, limiting what kind of content teens can see, and preventing strangers from sending them DMs. Meta says that it’s also started using Apple’s age-range signal as an additional detection method in Australia. Parents and guardians can also choose to supervise Teen Accounts to set time limits and monitor how their child is using Instagram. Teen Account settings can’t be adjusted by users who are 16 or younger without a parent’s or guardian’s permission. Meta says that parents in the US will start receiving a notification on Instagram next month that explains the age estimation process, and how they can ensure their teen’s age is accurately reflected on the platform. This global expansion follows a $17.1 billion lawsuit settlement in August in which Meta agreed to bolster its age assurance practices and place heavier restrictions on teen users. Meta says it’s in the process of rolling out its age estimation technology across Facebook, and that it will start launching similar tools for Threads later this year. Correction, November 9th: This article previously said the AI-powered age estimation tech was also used to detect and remove users who are under 13 years old, but Meta says this is a seperate process. The global expansion announced today will only place teen users under Teen Account settings.

articles.title: Pomera’s sleek distraction-free writing machine is just too small
articles.summary: The Pomera DM250 is the company’s first digital typewriter to reach the US. It has its charm, but it’s too uncomfortable for long typing sessions.
articles.body: Pomera’s digital typewriters are a cult hit with those craving a distraction-free writing experience. Dedicated word processor devices never caught on in the US the way they did in Japan. And the ones available in the US, like the AlphaSmart Neo, just weren’t as sleek and portable as the tiny foldable devices from Pomera. Until last year, Pomera devices were only available in Japan, leaving people to import them and stumble their way through software created for Japanese users. The $549 Pomera DM250US is the company’s first device created for US writers, with a US English keyboard layout and native English software. For those of us who want someplace to write where the temptation of Bluesky isn’t a click away and there’s no danger of disappearing down a Wikipedia rabbit hole, it was an exciting development. After months of testing, I can say that I get the appeal, but it’s not for me. The tradeoffs it makes to cram so much into such a portable device make it a literal pain to use for its intended purpose. [Product: Pomera DM250US | The DM250 is undeniably the sleekest distraction-free writing device I’ve come across. It’s a wide clamshell, with a serious-looking matte black finish and a 7-inch LCD screen that seems too small for its chassis. Its extremely compact size —10.3 inches wide, 4.7 inches deep, and 0.7 inches thick — means I can toss it in my tiny Uniqlo crossbody bag with room to spare for my Kobo, my iPod, two sets of headphones (wired and Bluetooth), plus a Field Notes and a pen. Its closest competitor is probably the Freewrite Traveler, which has a similar laptop-like form factor and price. The Traveler is larger in every direction, at 11.3 inches by 5 inches by 1 inch, and its glossy plastic feels cheap in comparison to the Pomera. The Traveler also opts for a crisp E Ink screen that sips battery life, but is also completely useless in a dimly lit room. Pomera’s battery life is pretty solid, though. It’s rated for 24 hours of continuous use. At least anecdotally, that seems to check out. I’ve been using Pomera sporadically for a little over three months now and have only had to charge it once. I last charged it in mid-September, and it’s still sitting at about 50 percent battery life. [Image: The Pomera is quite thin and portable. The software on the Pomera is also relatively complex for a distraction-free writing device. It has tons of options for customizing the interface, a basic calendar, and even spell check. I really like the calendar app. Each date has a text file associated with it that’s displayed in a sidebar. It’s easy to open quickly and add appointments, notes, or journal entries without closing the main document you’re working on. It’s the kind of perfect less-is-more tool that stays out of the way yet is incredibly flexible. Pomera also does have some welcome options for tweaking the interface. By default, it’s black text on a white screen, but you can invert that, which I found far more comfortable for long stretches of writing. There is a small status bar at the bottom that shows the file name, word count, battery level, and time, which you can hide by switching to full-screen mode. You can have ruled lines or even put a frame around your text to limit it to a particular part of the screen. Pomera’s editing tools are far more robust than its competitors, which tend to be no-frills plain text. You can place markers in your files and build an outline, insert a timestamp, or find and replace strings of text. You can insert templates, compare two files side by side, or even open the same file twice if you need to check multiple parts of a document at once. [Image: The tiny keyboard squeezes in a full set of function keys. Still, the Pomera just never clicked for me. That’s partly a software issue. The interface for writing on the device is thoughtful and feature-rich, but the two wireless syncing options are painful to use. The first is a finicky system for emailing work to yourself: You have to log in to a Gmail account and connect it to the Pomera to send text, which shows up in the body of the email, not as an attachment. (If you don’t have a Gmail account, you actually have to manually enter your SMTP info.) The other option is the convoluted Pomera Link mobile app. To use the app, you have to go to the menu on the Pomera itself and select QR code. Then you open the app and scan the code, which imports the text to your phone. But you can’t simply save it from there. Instead, you have to copy and paste the text into another app, like Google Docs, if you want to save it. It’s a mess. Thankfully, if you’ve got a USB-C cable, you can get your text off it by plugging your Pomera into a computer and transferring it like you would with any USB drive. The Pomera has a little over 1GB of built-in storage, which should be more than enough for most people — that will store hundreds of thousands of pages of plain text. But it also has an SD card slot if you’d prefer the convenience of storing your manuscripts there for easily moving between devices. [Image: A USB-C port and SD card slot can be found on the left side. But in the end, it wasn’t the Pomera’s software that sank it for me. Its keyboard is just too small. The size difference between the Traveler and the DM250US might seem negligible, but it’s painfully obvious the second you start typing. The Traveler features a full-size scissor-switch keyboard with a simplified design that ditches the function and arrow keys. Meanwhile, working with less space, Pomera squeezes in a full set of function keys and cursor keys. In small bursts, the keyboard isn’t terrible. I won’t be writing any odes to its keys’ shallow yet satisfying action, but I’ve definitely used worse. The thing is, my hands start to cramp, and my wrists hurt pretty quickly. My hands are not particularly large, but the layout and tiny keys are an absolute nightmare for my carpal tunnel. I wrote this review on the Pomera and had to take breaks every 300 words or so because it was just too uncomfortable to keep going for much longer, and its small size meant I also made a lot more typos than usual. If you’ve got particularly small hands it might not be as much of an issue. [Image: The utilitarian look gives Pomera a more premium vibe than many of its competitors. Don’t get fooled by the “Bluetooth keyboard” option in the menu — it doesn’t mean you can connect an external keyboard to the Pomera. Instead, this allows you to use the Pomera as a keyboard with other devices, which I guess could be helpful in a pinch. If you were going to use a Bluetooth keyboard anyway, it might be worth looking into BYOK, which, as the name implies, lets you bring your keyboard. It’s quite a bit cheaper than the Pomera, even if its editing features are less robust. If portability was my number one priority, and I didn’t want to resort to some clunky folding keyboard, the Pomera would fit the bill. It feels sturdier and more premium than its most obvious competitor, the Traveler, and as much as I like the BYOK, that’s definitely got a bit of an amateurish vibe by comparison. Ultimately, though, the biggest problem is simply ergonomic. The whole draw of devices like the Pomera DM250US is sitting down for long, serious writing sessions. But inevitably, every time I’d use it, I’d find myself reaching for my wrist braces and doing finger stretches afterward. It doesn’t matter how sleek and portable Pomera’s design is, or how much I appreciated its more advanced editing features or its flexible calendar — discomfort is its own distraction.

articles.title: Uber wants to park your car now, too
articles.summary: Uber is launching Uber Parking across 15 US cities, letting drivers reserve and pay for spots in-app using SpotHero’s 13,000-facility network.
articles.body: Uber announced the launch of Uber Parking, a native in-app reservation feature that allows drivers to find, book, and pay for garage and lot spaces ahead of time. The new feature is a result of Uber’s recent acquisition of SpotHero, integrating a network of over 13,000 facilities across more than 400 cities into the company’s platform. The new feature works by tapping the new “Parking” icon in the Uber app to view an interactive map with upfront prices and arrival times. You can filter spots by self-park or valet, outdoor lot or garage, and whether staff are on-site. The app will prompt you to enter your vehicle details and license plate, after which can enter certain lots using a QR code on your phone or through an automatic license plate scan. If your plans change, you can extend your time directly in the app or cancel for free right up until your reservation starts. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Uber One subscribers can earn 10 percent back on parking reservations as account credits within 24 hours. These credits can then be spent on rides or Uber Eats deliveries. Uber says that its subscription service has grown to more than 55 million members across 47 countries as of late 2026. Uber Parking is launching in 15 initial markets, including Chicago, NYC, Boston, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Washington D.C., Atlanta, Austin, Dallas, Denver, Miami, Nashville, Philadelphia, San Diego, and Seattle — eventually rolling out to SpotHero’s existing 400-city footprint. The move also ties directly into Uber’s wider bet on robotaxis, working with over 30 autonomous vehicle partners across multiple cities. In the long run, these 13,000-plus parking facilities won’t just hold commuter cars — Uber plans to turn them into urban holding pens and waiting areas for driverless robotaxis. Stashing autonomous fleets off the street when demand dips helps keep empty cars from aimlessly circling city blocks, cutting down on traffic, emissions, and wear on the vehicles, Uber says. Ultimately, it shows that the company is thinking bigger than just ride-hailing and delivery — it wants to control the city’s physical roads and parking spaces, regardless of whether the person traveling is driving their own car, riding in the backseat, or letting a computer take the wheel. By getting into parking, Uber is also tacitly admitting that its earlier mission to end personal car ownership and driver’s licenses didn’t succeed. But there is a loyalty-retaining strategy at play here, too, with Uber intent on keeping its customers operating within in its own platform ecosystem, whether they’re hailing a ride or driving their own car.

articles.title: Phones to be banned from pupils' bags or pockets under new rules
articles.summary: The government says it is strengthening its guidance for schools in England, which came into force in June.
articles.body:
Pupils will not be allowed to have their phones on them at all during the school day under stricter government guidance in England.

Statutory guidance came into force in June, making schools and trusts legally responsible for being phone-free throughout the day.

Ministers now say changes to that guidance will go beyond the current "no see, no hear" policies in place in some schools - where phones can remain in pupils' bags if they are not seen or heard - when it comes into force from September 2027.

But head teachers' unions said schools would struggle to implement stricter new policies without additional funding from government.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell said the government's "clear message" to parents and pupils was that "school is for learning and friendship, not scrolling".

Access to phones "risks pulling children away from their learning and from each other", the government said.

Schools will be able to decide how to follow the guidance. Some schools have invested in sealed pouches or secure lockers. Others collect phones at the start of the day, or have prohibited them from sites altogether.

Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the NAHT school leaders union, said phones could raise "safety issues" and be an "unhelpful distraction" during the school day. But he said the more robust measures recommended under the new guidance would "come at a cost".

Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said the latest guidance "does at least provide some clarity", but added that school leaders "cannot simply make mobile phones disappear".

"If all schools are going to be expected to have lockable pouches or other secure storage facilities for every pupil, the cost involved will be very significant indeed," he said.

"This is not feasible unless the government puts in the funding required to meet these costs."

Dame Rachel de Souza, Children's Commissioner for England, said she welcomed strong action to stop phones distracting pupils and disrupting the school day.

Charlotte Ashton, co-founder of campaign group of Generation Focus, similarly welcomed the changes, saying "no see, no hear" policies were not working and pupils were still "TikToking in the toilets".

"Ultimately, we need to get to a point where it's not normal for every single child to have a personal internet-enabled device in their pockets with them 24/7," she said.

Shadow Education Secretary Laura Trott said she was "delighted that Labour have finally listened to us and agreed to properly ban smartphones in schools".

She said it was also the "right thing to do" to have a review of safety standards around the technology used in schools, which the government has also announced on the back of calls for improved guidance .

But she criticised what she called a lack of "joined up thinking" over what new tech was being allowed in classrooms.

Because education is devolved, the approach to phones in schools varies across the UK.

In Scotland , the government has said it will introduce a new law to restrict the personal use of phones in schools, and launched a consultation on the issue over the summer.

In Wales , the Senedd recently voted against a motion to introduce a national statutory ban on phones in classrooms. Schools are still encouraged to restrict the use of phones during the school day, but heads have flexibility over how to implement their own rules.

And in Northern Ireland , Education Minister Paul Givan launched a 12-week consultation in August on whether to ban mobile phones from schools by law, calling for "a stronger and more consistent approach across our education system".

Rules around phones in schools are separate from the UK's upcoming ban on social media for under-16s, due to be introduced in March.

Children will be barred from accessing platforms like Instagram, Snapchat and TikTok. Vinted and eBay could also be included in the list of platforms set to be banned, the culture secretary has said.

Additional reporting by Beth Rose and Nathan Standley

articles.title: Olivia Cooke Says ‘House of the Dragon’ Fandom Led Her to Step Away From Social Media: ‘There’s a Lot of Ugliness,’ ‘Misogyny’ and ‘Racism’
articles.summary: Olivia Cooke, who plays the controversial Queen Alicent Hightower in HBO’s “Game of Thrones” prequel “House of the Dragon,” recently told GQ that she stepped...
articles.body:
Olivia Cooke, who plays the controversial Queen Alicent Hightower in HBO's "Game of Thrones" prequel "House of the Dragon," recently told GQ that she stepped away from social media ahead of the show's third season because of the fandom's "ugliness."

"I think some of those interpretations just catch fire, and they become something that bears no resemblance to what was shown on the screen at the time," said Cooke on the subject of the fanbases' theories and opinions (which include observations about Cooke herself as well as her relationship with the show's directors). The uber-passionate fanbase was, in part, why she went offline and deactivated her Instagram ahead of Season 3 dropping in June, she revealed. "There's a lot of ugliness to that fandom as well. It's steeped in misogyny. There's a lot of racism. I try to let it take up minimal mental real estate."

While viewers of the prequel series are well-acquainted with the taboo at this point, Season 3 saw Cooke's Hightower in a number of contentious storylines, including sharing a kiss with her son that results in an incestuous daydream scene later on.

On the subject of her social media break, the actress noted that it got to a place where she felt it was "not nourishing." "I think the celebri-fied nature of being an actor has now snowballed into this monster. And I just think we need to get off this train and realize that we make these TV shows and films, yes, for escapism, but also because it's artful and it's creative and it's not for followers or for a brand deal or to get free shit. Even though that is nice sometimes."

As for her relationship with director Clare Kilner, Cooke told the magazine that Kilner proves "you don't have to stomp around the set and exert testosterone. You can just handle each department with kindness and care."

"House of the Dragon" first aired on HBO in 2022. The prequel series earned three Golden Globe nominations and one win for best television series, drama. It's been nominated for 14 Emmys and won 2: outstanding fantasy/sci-fi costumes in 2023 and outstanding period or fantasy/sci-fi makeup (non-prosthetic) in 2025.

articles.title: Seagate’s FireCuda Forge moves your data between a hard drive and SSD for better performance
articles.summary: Seagate’s FireCuda Forge dynamically moves your data between a hard drive and SSD so the files you currently need the most are more quickly accessible.
articles.body: Seagate announced a new external storage solution, called the FireCuda Forge, that combines the speed benefits of an SSD with the affordability of a higher-capacity hard drive. The Forge is the first drive that’s powered by the company’s new Alkemi intelligent storage platform, which learns how your data is used and relocates the files you’re currently using, or use most frequently, to the faster SSD. The FireCuda Forge is now available through Seagate’s online store with an 8TB hard drive for $699, or a 20TB hard drive for $899, that are both user-replaceable. However, the NVMe SSD is not included, and in the middle of a memory shortage, that will significantly add to the Forge’s price. Combining a hard drive with flash storage isn’t a new idea. Seagate has been selling hybrid drives with flash memory built in for decades. The Forge lets users choose what hard drive and SSD they want to use together. It sounds similar to network attached storage (NAS) solutions that let you add an SSD where frequently accessed data is temporarily cached, but Seagate says its new FireCuda Forge works differently. The Alkemi technology uses machine learning to dynamically move data from one drive to the other based on your current workload and what data that requires. As your needs and tasks change, the data will be dynamically reorganized across the two drives but will always appear as just a single drive connected to your PC. The FireCuda Forge offers read speeds up to 2,500MB/s and write speeds that top out at 2,000MB/s on computers running at least Windows 11 or macOS 26.

The conversation started after people noticed Qazi’s reaction to singer Jasmine Sandlas performing a song from Dhurandhar, with a post going viral about his reaction and sparking speculation online.But Aasif had a different take on the conversation, relating it to his own experience of sharing the Bigg Boss house with Qazi. Much love and power to you @qazitouqeer_official”What is striking about Aasif’s message is its focus on seeing the moment through the artist’s eyes, rather than judging it from assumptions. articles.title: Amazon turned its Alexa robot into a Ring security patrol bot
articles.summary: Amazon’s new Ring Rover Cam repurposes its Astro home robot as an autonomous roaming security camera for businesses.
articles.body: As part of a new brand called Ring Robotics — designed to take a more proactive approach to security instead of just monitoring — a new rolling mobile security camera was announced by Amazon, called the Ring Rover Cam. It borrows a lot of the design and functionality from the Astro home robot that Amazon first debuted in 2021. The Rover Cam is targeted at businesses in need of an affordable security solution that can patrol and investigate concerns in large facilities, and it comes with a few upgrades. As with Astro, the Rover Cam rolls around on a pair of large wheels that help it navigate small obstacles or uneven terrain. It can be manually dispatched to a specific room or any point along a pre-programmed patrol route to investigate a disturbance, and it will also automatically head to a location where an alarm on another Ring device is triggered. While en route, it continuously streams and records video, and when it reaches its destination, the robot performs a 360-degree scan so you can investigate what’s wrong from afar. [Image: The Rover Cam relies more heavily on its telescoping periscope camera than Astro did. Astro’s extending periscope camera has been carried forward to the Rover Cam and upgraded. It now features 4K resolution, and you can set the camera to raise and lower to specific heights while programming a scheduled patrol route so the robot can see over counters, shelving, or other raised obstacles. Astro’s cupholder has been replaced with a permanent stubby tower featuring a built-in siren and a flashing red light that both function as deterrents. To make the Rover Cam easier to locate in large spaces like a warehouse, that tower also projects a blue ring of light onto ceilings directly above the robot. [Image: The Rover Cam’s screen is used to provide status messages, including letting others know when it’s recording video. There’s no access to Alexa through the Rover Cam, which makes its included screen feel unnecessary. Instead of displaying a cute pair of eyes to encourage engagement, the Rover Cam’s screen is used to display status messages, including when it’s actively recording. It still has a microphone and speakers, but now they’re used for two-way talk functionality. Battery life is estimated to be about 30 minutes, allowing the robot to cover facilities around 5,000 square feet, but it’s limited to a single floor. For multiple levels, multiple robots would be needed, or the Rover Cam can be paired with Amazon’s new flying Ring Drone Cam. [Media: This isn’t the first time that Amazon has attempted to repurpose Astro as a security robot. In 2023, it launched the $2,349.99 Astro for Business but discontinued it just a year later. The Ring Rover Cam is now available for preorder for $999.99 and is expected to ship starting on December 16th.

articles.title: Hands-on with Ring’s new AI drone camera for your home
articles.summary: Ring’s $249.99 Drone Cam is a flying indoor security camera piloted by cloud-based AI, set to ship on January 27th, 2027. We went hands-on at the launch.
articles.body: Ring is finally shipping a flying indoor drone camera. For real this time. The Ring Drone Cam will arrive on January 27th, 2027, for $249.99, Ring founder Jamie Siminoff said at a launch event in New York City this week. If it does actually ship, it will arrive almost six years after the company announced its first flying camera, the Ring Always Home Cam. Designed to patrol inside your home when you’re not there, the Drone Cam is an AI-powered drone that can react to triggers from Ring sensors, such as detecting motion, a door opening, a water leak, or an alarm sounding. When triggered, it flies along preprogrammed routes to a set location, where it can livestream and record what’s happening in the Ring app. The drone can also run scheduled patrols around your home or be sent out on demand. It offers 2K resolution, a 148-degree field of view, and, because it’s mobile, it can cover 360 degrees. The Verge got some hands-on time with the new flying camera at the launch event. [Image: The Drone Cam is small and very lightweight at 165 grams. [Image: It has no onboard sensors beyond those required for landing. It relies on AI to fly. [Image: This is its charging dock. [Image: When docked, the drone’s camera is fully covered. Ring’s pitch here is that the Drone Cam can replace the need for multiple cameras in your home while still letting you see what’s happening anywhere in your home if there’s an incident. It is designed for indoor use only, and the company claims it has built-in privacy: It records only while flying. The drone’s camera is shuttered when it’s docked, and it’s noisy as heck when it’s flying, so there’s no way it could sneak up and invade your privacy. [Image: Ring founder Jamie Siminoff demoing the Drone Cam in New York City. Footage from the Drone Cam is encrypted using Ring’s new TAKE (Throw Away the Key Encryption) system, which rotates encryption keys every five minutes and deletes Ring’s copies after 24 hours, limiting Amazon’s access while still allowing cloud processing for features like smart alerts and AI-powered video search. [Media: At the event, I saw the Drone Cam take flight and got some hands-on time with the device. It’s a completely different product from the Always Home Cam that was announced in 2020. It’s significantly smaller, about a quarter the size of the model I saw demoed at CES in 2023, weighing 165 grams. A small camera is integrated into its body, as opposed to dangling in the center. [Video: Ring Drone Cam Footage of Jen] Ring claims the Drone Cam can fly for five to eight minutes on a charge, and for every minute of flight time, it takes eight minutes of charging — that means a five-minute flight needs about 40 minutes of charging. This short flight time suggests the product is better suited to quick check-ins than continuous monitoring, and whether it can really replace multiple stationary cameras remains to be seen. At this week’s demo, I saw it complete a 1-minute flight, taking off from its dock, hovering, then following a pre-planned route around a simple living room layout. Unlike the CES demo, this time I was able to see the drone take off and land several times, then navigate smoothly with barely any wobble. [Image: Me checking out the Ring Drone Cam. According to Ring, the Drone Cam can fly up stairs and uses LED spotlights to help it see in the dark and deter potential intruders — but Ring didn’t demo this. The drone apparently follows preplanned flight paths you set up in the Ring app and will go around any obstacles it encounters along those routes. However, I didn’t get to see it interact with obstacles or anything unexpected — I’m particularly curious how pets will react to it. A long runway Siminoff said Ring has been developing the drone since 2016 and has come close to shipping two different models over that time before landing on the current version. Siminoff explained that they struggled to pack all the technology needed for an autonomous drone to fly in your home into a practical design for less than $250. About a year ago, they decided to start from scratch and build a much more basic drone that could fly reliably while putting its brains in the cloud. [Image: The Drone Cam in flight. Ring developed AI Pilot, a new AI system that combines the device’s camera with vision models, sensors, and cloud processing to map your home and let the drone navigate autonomously around obstacles, while relying on preprogrammed routes. “Truly, it’s like an AI agent that’s controlling the robot,” said Siminoff. The downside is that it depends entirely on an internet connection, which is a potential failure point for a home security product; without Wi-Fi, all it can do is land. [Image: Siminoff also announced the Ring Rover Cam (left) alongside the Ring Drone Cam (right) this week. The Drone Cam launches in the US only as part of a new Ring Robotics line alongside the Ring Rover Cam, a $999.99 autonomous security robot for businesses built on Amazon’s Astro home robot. Rover also uses AI Pilot and is available for preorder now, with shipping expected to begin on December 16th, 2026. Both security devices work like any other Ring camera, streaming and sending recorded video to the Ring app and requiring a Ring Protect plan for video storage and advanced features. They will also work with Amazon’s upcoming Alexa Home Map to understand your home and where sensors and other devices are located. [Image: Ring’s Drone Cam is slated to launch in January. It will be available in gray. Although Siminoff seemed confident the drone will launch in January as planned, Ring says it is currently “in the process of obtaining FCC certification.” When asked about the FCC’s ban on foreign-made drones, Siminoff said Ring Drone Cam “does comply with” FCC regulations and noted it’s assembled in the US. It’s normal for new gadgets to go through this process, but drones now face extra scrutiny. Ring ushered in a world of new privacy questions when its cameras first started entering people’s homes more than a decade ago. Over the past year, the company’s new technologies have sparked fears that it could enable a surveillance state. An AI-piloted drone that can map your home, fly from room to room, and relies on the cloud to operate will certainly raise new privacy questions when it hits the market next year. Photos by Victoria Barrios / The Verge

articles.title: Aura’s next color E Ink photo frame is smaller, cheaper, sharper, and more colorful
articles.summary: The Aura Ink is now available with a smaller 10-inch color E Ink screen that delivers performance upgrades and a cheaper price.
articles.body: Aura just launched a smaller version of its color E Ink frame with a handful of improvements and a more affordable price. The new Aura Ink frame features a 10-inch E Ink panel that can display more colors at a higher pixel density. It’s also differentiated from the original 13-inch model with a black frame and matching mat board that helps photos stand out. The Aura Ink 10 is now available in the US for $349, $150 cheaper than the 13-inch version, which still costs $499. The original Ink’s price made it a tough sell over Aura’s other frames that are available with an LCD screen as large as 15 inches for $299. The new 10-inch option makes color E Ink more accessible, and it carries forward one of the Ink’s biggest advantages: a rechargeable battery so the frame can hang on a wall without a dangling power cord. [Product: Aura Ink 10-inch | Although color E Ink displays have been available in e-readers like Kindles and Kobos for a few years, those devices use a color filter over a standard black-and-white e-paper panel with limited color reproduction. The Aura Ink instead uses E Ink’s Spectra 6 technology, which creates patterns of black, white, red, yellow, blue, and green ink droplets to reproduce a much wider color spectrum. [Image: The new 10-inch version of the Aura Ink frame is sharper than the original, but up close you can still easily see the dithered patterns of colored dots that make up each image. For the new 10-inch version, Aura worked with E Ink to add three custom base colors created by mixing those six inks in new ways: off-white, mustard yellow, and orange. The goal was to improve the company’s proprietary dithering algorithm to produce more natural-looking colors on faces, add detail to textures like grass, and to help smooth gradients so photos of sunsets, for example, look better. The 10-inch panel also has a higher pixel density — 200ppi, up from 150ppi on the 13-inch model — allowing it to produce slightly sharper results. Both are welcome improvements, but in practice the color reproduction isn’t drastically better than the original. You’d need to compare the same photo on both models side by side to really see a difference, and the upgrades don’t overcome one of the major shortcomings of the Spectra 6 technology. While E Ink estimates it can reproduce around 65,000 different colors — and potentially even more with Aura’s enhancements — LCD displays can produce millions. [Image: The bright yellow color of this water taxi looked very desaturated on the Aura Ink. It’s hard to know how well photos will be reproduced on its color E Ink screen. That can make it hard to predict how your photos will look on the new Aura Ink. Rich colors — like blue sky, green trees, and bright red flags — really pop, but skin tones can still sometimes look too warm or cold. I sent to the frame a photo of a bright-yellow water taxi photographed on a sunny day and expected it to appear well saturated, but that particular shade of yellow came out disappointingly subdued. The technology still has its challenges, but the benefits of E Ink’s color displays make the new Aura Ink a tempting alternative to the company’s LCD-based frames, particularly for those who don’t want another glowing screen at home. Photos displayed on the Aura Ink look like a printed photo, even with a subtle front light that automatically adjusts to boost the lighting in a room. [Image: Refreshing the photo displayed on the Aura Ink is a process that takes about 30 seconds with waves of color that ripple and flicker across its E Ink screen. It would fit right in on a wall of printed photos, and Aura estimates you’d need to take it down every three months to charge. But that’s if you update the displayed photo once every night. You can increase the frequency through Aura’s mobile app to up to 12 automatic refreshes per day, or manually change it using a set of buttons hidden on the back if you don’t mind charging the Ink more often. Just be mindful that unlike an e-reader that refreshes a page of text in less than a second, it takes the Ink about 30 seconds to change to a new image after a series of flickering, psychedelic patterns. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: I’ve been testing it as a standalone picture frame using a removable support that props the Aura Ink up in landscape or horizontal orientations. Moving it around the house without hunting for an outlet first is a big plus. And as with all of Aura’s digital photo frames, the new 10-inch Ink also benefits from the polished mobile app that has helped make the company’s products so popular. You can send photos to the Ink through a Wi-Fi connection with free, unlimited cloud storage or create shared albums that friends and family can view and contribute to. It also works with Google Photos and Apple Photos. If you don’t have access to the app, you can text or email photos directly to the frame. [Image: If you don’t want another bright glowing screen in your home, Aura’s new Ink makes E Ink’s color screen technology more affordable and accessible. If you plan to gift an Aura frame during the holidays, the company’s LCD models are still more budget-friendly, with 10-inch options starting at $149. The new version of the Aura Ink still feels like a device for early adopters who completely understand the tradeoffs of E Ink’s color screens. But if you prefer the look of printed photos over a glowing LCD, the smaller Aura Ink is now one of the most affordable ways to try out this tech. Photography by Andrew Liszewski / The Verge

articles.title: Aura's newest e-ink photo frame is even better and more affordable than its last | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Aura is unveiling a new product: a 10-inch digital e-ink frame that can blend in seamlessly with printed photos.
articles.body:
If you’re into interior design, decorating, or just love displaying your family photos, Aura ‘s latest product line will feel magical. Aura’s cordless Ink photo frames have the versatility of a digital photo frame, but their e-ink displays don’t even look digital, blending seamlessly into the rest of your framed photos.

A follow-up to its 13-inch, $499 Ink frame , Aura is unveiling a new product that’s a little less pricey: a 10-inch Ink frame that is now on sale for $349.

“Ten years ago when we were first starting Aura, we were interested in making an e-ink picture frame. We just wanted a frame that looked like a printed photo and magically changed, but the tech was not there at that point,” Aura co-founder and CTO Eric Jensen told TechCrunch. “So it’s great to be able to see it moving forward.”

Aura uses E Ink’s Spectra 6 display for its Ink frames, which can only render six different colors. What sets Aura apart is its proprietary dithering algorithm, a technique that blends a limited color palette into patterns that the eye reads as smooth gradients.

While the 13″ Ink frame looks beautiful, it is obvious that the colors are not exact to the original photo. For the new 10″ Ink frame, Aura worked with E Ink on expanding its Spectra 6 technology to incorporate three new proprietary colors: off white, mustard, and orange.

“The net effect is that the edges are smoothed a bit more,” Jensen said. “You can see if you zoom in on a face, the places where we would’ve had to previously put white next to red, or something a little more jarring, we can now fill in with the right color, and it effectively makes it a little bit higher resolution.”

With the extra three colors, the Ink 10″ is getting truer to representing an original photo, but the colors still appear less saturated on the digital display than in a printed image.

For both Ink frames, Aura paid special attention to rendering skin tones accurately, since most people use these frames for family photos. (Personally, I think the slight variations in color give scenery photos a cool, vintage look.) It may not matter as much if your kid’s bright pink shirt looks closer to red on the Ink, but if her skin is unnaturally grey, then it would look pretty weird, hence Aura’s meticulous calibration of these colors.

The 10″ frame only comes in one colorway: a black frame with a dark grey linen-textured mat. It looks a bit jarring at first, and I wouldn’t hang it on a gallery wall next to 10 other white-matted photos, but it looks great on its own.

“We intentionally made it dark so that it didn’t have as much contrast with the e-ink display next to it,” Jensen said.

Like Aura’s other frames, the Ink 10″ is compatible with Aura’s app, where customers and their family and friends can easily upload photos from their phone to an album of photos that display on their frame.

“On average, there’s about four people sharing to each frame,” Jensen said, meaning that it’s common for customers to share their Aura albums with others. If your mother has an Aura frame, for example, she can grant you permission to add photos to her frame, letting you easily drop the newest photos of her grandson at the park.

On Ink frames, the company recommends setting the frame to only update once per day, since changing photos consumes battery life (and it’s a bit odd to watch the dithering algorithm in action).

Aura comes with hanging hardware, a stand, and a USB-C charging cable, and the company claims that the Ink 10″ can last three months on a single charge. In my experience with the Ink 13″, I’d say the battery actually lasts about a month. But this is perhaps because I had displayed it in an area of my home that gets a lot of light, so the front light is probably lit more often than if I had placed it elsewhere.

The new Ink frame still doesn’t generate perfect, one-to-one reproductions of your photos, but the precision of color doesn’t matter that much. What matters more is that, if you aren’t expecting it, you could easily be fooled into thinking that the Ink 10″ is just an ordinary framed photo.

articles.title: Google broadens its AI hardware portfolio with two new specialized chips | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Google's new tensor processing units (TPUs) broaden its chip portfolio to more use cases: confidential model training and more memory capacity.
articles.body:
Google is notching up its chipmaking game as the company seeks to reduce its dependence on chips made by other companies for its cloud computing business. Google on Monday unveiled two new variants of its tensor processing units (TPUs), in-house-developed chips meant for AI workloads, that broaden its chip portfolio to additional use cases: confidential inference and more memory capacity for large workloads.

The new units, TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, are part of the company’s eighth generation of chips introduced in April this year, and build on what those chips offered, which was more inference capacity and support for large training requirements.

TPU 8tx, designed with AMD, is based on the TPU 8t chip, and is geared specifically for confidentially training and running AI models, Google said in a blog post. The chip “builds security directly into the hardware layer, keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use,” the company wrote.

The chip also has a custom inferencing network that lets it run reasoning alongside training, so it can be used to distill and train small models on the fly. That ability, according to Google, could prove useful for cases where a company might want to train a model on its proprietary data without having to move the data between devices.

Meanwhile, TPU 8i Max basically combines two of the inference-focused TPU 8i chips the company launched in April, doubling the memory capacity, processing power and bandwidth, but in a single package. The result is a chip that lets AI models handle a larger range of information during queries.

The chip launch comes as hyperscalers like Microsoft , Amazon , and even AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic are working on their own lines of AI-specific semiconductors and accompanying software in order to reduce their reliance on the dominance of Nvidia.

The news also comes at a particularly vulnerable moment for Nvidia, whose CEO Jensen Huang over the weekend admitted to having an affair with someone alleged to be a Chinese spy.

articles.title: Google Fi is bringing back multiple cell network support for better coverage
articles.summary: Google Fi is bringing back support for connecting to multiple networks and will automatically switch users on newer Pixel phones to whichever one is faster.
articles.body: Google Fi is launching a new “super network” that can automatically switch users between two different 5G networks depending on which one has better connectivity. The feature is rolling out starting today on Pixel 9 and newer phones that have Google Fi active on eSIM and have any non-Fi SIMs disabled. When Google Fi first launched in 2015, users were originally able to switch between T-Mobile and Sprint’s networks. But those two networks eventually became one when T-Mobile acquired Sprint in 2020, and so the network switching stopped there. Jane Harnett, Google Fi Wireless senior product manager, told The Verge that Fi stopped offering the feature because “the wireless landscape consolidated via mergers and limited our ability to offer multiple networks within the US.” (Networking switching has continued to be available internationally.) Now the feature is returning to the US, with Fi once again hopping between two networks. Harnett declined to share which networks Fi will be working with to make this happen. Google Fi’s FAQs say it currently provides coverage through T-Mobile’s network. According to Harnett, Google Fi’s new approach to network switching is faster than what it offered before, and uses eSIMs’ ability to connect to multiple carriers at once: > “Previously Fi’s switching was single-SIM switching which could only connect to one network at a time, so your phone had to wait until service dropped completely before performing a slow SIM profile swap into another network without knowing if coverage was actually better there. Fi also tried dual-SIM iterations that required both a physical SIM and eSIM which could be slower to transition. > Now we are back with added networks domestically. We have rebuilt the experience from the ground up for the modern era. With our new switching on newer Pixel devices, your phone keeps two eSIM network profiles on standby at the same time (via MEP technology) and uses the Android OS to monitor live connection quality. It also lets your phone transition faster and more fluidly with minimal battery impact—knowing a better connection is available before it switches.”

articles.title: Pixel Tag, Google's $30 Android-ready answer to Apple's AirTag, is now available | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Google's Pixel Tag lets you track lost items with your Android device, similar to Apple's AirTag.
articles.body:
Google’s answer to Apple’s AirTag, the Google Pixel Tag , goes on sale starting Tuesday, allowing Android users to track items like their keys, wallet, or bag using their smartphone’s built-in Find Hub.

First announced in August , the $29.99 device takes cues from the AirTag and other lost-item finders by offering connectivity via Bluetooth and ultra-wideband for precision finding. This lets Android device owners, including Pixel Watch wearers, locate their missing items using a combination of visual distance and directional guidance.

Plus, the tag has a built-in speaker to play a chime that helps you locate your item if nearby. (Or, if you’ve lost your phone, you can press the button on the Pixel Tag twice to ring it, too.) You can choose between three different levels of loudness in the settings within the Find Hub, with the maximum volume around 80 decibels.

Though the Pixel Tag serves the same purpose as an AirTag, Google has opted for a different design. Instead of a small, round device, like Apple’s, the Pixel Tag is slimmer and more elongated.

Spec-by-spec, the Pixel Tag is 1.1-inches wide, compared to the AirTag’s 1.26 inches. As the Pixel Tag is oval-shaped, it’s 1.8-inches high from top to bottom. Thickness-wise, the Pixel Tag clocks in at a depth of 0.2 inches, compared with the AirTag’s 0.31 inches (which Apple calls its height). The slimness of the device might make it more appealing for some, particularly if they’re adding the tag to a small item, like a keychain.

The device weighs just 0.4 oz, with the battery included.

Unlike Apple, Google opted for a physical button you can press on the tag, which makes it more obvious how it’s meant to work.

Google didn’t originally say that the Pixel Tag included NFC when it announced the device in August. NFC is used by Apple’s AirTag to aid people who find lost items, as they can tap the side of the tag to launch a webpage that displays the owner’s contact information. Google uses the tap gesture to instead connect the user to the device’s settings.

Meanwhile, for lost items that are not nearby, the Pixel Tag relies on Google’s crowdsourced network of over a billion Android devices globally. The network, similar to competitive offerings from Apple and Tile, taps into the connectivity provided by other Android devices, which can identify and share the location of the lost item back to its owner. This location information is displayed on a map inside the Find Hub app.

While the person who found the item can’t tap it, as with NFC-enabled devices, Pixel Tags that are put into “Lost” mode will be able to share the owner’s email, number, and a short message so the person who finds the tag can contact you. When the tag comes back into range of the user’s phone, the item is automatically marked as found.

The Pixel Tag’s location can also be shared with up to 10 people in the Find Hub app, which could be useful for shared items like the family car keys, which multiple people might rely on.

Like AirTag, the Pixel Tag is powered by a user-replaceable coin cell battery (the CR2032), which makes the device reusable for the long term. (Google claims the device has up to one year of battery life to start.)

Meanwhile, the device itself is made from stainless steel and features IP67 water and dust resistance (maximum depth of 1 meter up to 30 minutes). It pairs with devices running Android 9 or newer via Fast Pair technology.

The Pixel Tag comes in two shades: silver and a pale green, and can be bought individually or in a four-pack for $99.99.

Alongside the launch, the company Bellroy is debuting its own keychain cases in a variety of colors and styles, which will also be sold on the Google Store.

Post updated after publication to note that the Pixel Tag now supports NFC, which was a surprise addition not mentioned at the time of its announcement.
